title: Architecture for Accessibility and Inclusion
objectives: Ensure architecture decisions support accessible, inclusive services
Understand the legal obligations under the Public Sector Bodies Accessibility Regulations 2018
Design architectures that enable WCAG 2.2 AA compliance by default
Make architecture decisions that support assisted digital and offline access
Embed accessibility as a systemic property rather than a surface-level concern
whyThisMatters:
In the UK, one in five people have a long-term impairment affecting their ability to do everyday activities. Government services are often the only way to access critical support — benefits, healthcare, legal processes. When these services are not accessible, people are excluded from things they have a legal right to access.

This is not just a moral concern — it is a legal one. The Public Sector Bodies (Websites and Mobile Applications) Accessibility Regulations 2018 require public sector websites and mobile applications to meet the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 at AA standard. The Equality Act 2010 places a duty on public authorities to make reasonable adjustments for disabled people. Non-compliance carries legal, reputational, and political risk.

Most accessibility guidance focuses on design and development: use sufficient colour contrast, provide alt text for images, ensure keyboard navigation works. These are essential but insufficient. Accessibility is also an architecture concern. The choices you make about technology stack, API design, content management, notification channels, and progressive enhancement determine whether accessibility is achievable at all — or whether the development team is fighting against the architecture to make things accessible.

content.heading: Accessibility as an Architecture Concern
content.body:
Accessibility is typically treated as a front-end concern — a matter of HTML, CSS, and ARIA attributes. But architecture decisions made long before any HTML is written determine whether a service can be made accessible or not.

Technology selection shapes accessibility. A service built entirely as a single-page application with client-side rendering may struggle with screen readers unless significant additional work is done to manage focus and announce dynamic content. A service using the GOV.UK Design System and progressive enhancement will be accessible by default because the patterns have been tested with assistive technologies.

API design shapes accessibility. An API that only returns data in complex nested JSON structures forces the front-end to do heavy processing, making it harder to create simple, accessible interfaces. An API designed with the front-end in mind — providing data in the shape the interface needs — enables cleaner, more accessible implementations.

Content architecture shapes accessibility. A system that stores content as formatted HTML limits how that content can be presented across different channels and assistive technologies. A system that stores content as structured data with semantic meaning can render it appropriately for any context — web, screen reader, braille display, or plain text.

Notification architecture shapes accessibility. A system that only notifies users via email excludes users who cannot read emails without assistance. A system designed to notify through multiple channels (email, SMS, letter, in-app) with user preference allows people to choose the channel that works for them.

Authentication architecture shapes accessibility. A system that requires users to read a code from an authenticator app excludes users who cannot see the screen. A system offering multiple authentication methods (app, SMS, security key, phone call) enables users to choose what works with their abilities.

The key insight: accessibility is a systemic property of the architecture, not a decorative layer applied to the surface. If the architecture makes accessibility difficult, no amount of front-end effort will fully compensate.

content.heading: Legal Obligations and Government Standards
content.body:
The legal landscape for accessibility in UK government is clear and increasingly enforced.

The Public Sector Bodies (Websites and Mobile Applications) Accessibility Regulations 2018 require all public sector websites and mobile applications to meet WCAG 2.2 at level AA. This is not guidance — it is law. The Government Digital Service monitors compliance and can require organisations to fix accessibility issues. Non-compliance can result in enforcement action and reputational damage.

WCAG 2.2, published in October 2023 and adopted as the UK government standard, includes nine new success criteria beyond WCAG 2.1. Key additions relevant to architecture include: Dragging Movements (2.5.7) — functionality that uses dragging must have a single-pointer alternative; Target Size (2.5.8) — interactive targets must be at least 24x24 CSS pixels; and Consistent Help (3.2.6) — help mechanisms must appear in the same relative location across pages.

The Service Standard requires services to be accessible and inclusive (Point 5). Service assessments specifically examine accessibility compliance, and services that do not demonstrate accessibility testing and remediation will not pass assessment.

The Digital Assurance Playbook explicitly includes accessibility as an area that assurers should check. Legally, public sector websites and apps must meet accessibility standards, and suppliers have a legal duty to make their technology accessible.

Beyond legal compliance, the GDS accessibility guidance emphasises that accessibility is about inclusion — designing for the full diversity of users from the start, not retrofitting for compliance. An accessibility statement must be published for every public-facing service, describing the service's accessibility status and known issues.

For architects, the practical implication is: accessibility must be a design constraint from day one, not a testing concern at the end. If your architecture does not support accessibility, your service cannot comply with the law — regardless of how good your development team is.

content.heading: Architecture Decisions That Enable Accessibility
content.body:
Several architectural choices make accessibility easier to achieve and maintain.

Progressive enhancement as the default architecture: Build the core experience using HTML that works without JavaScript, then enhance with JavaScript for users whose browsers support it. This ensures the service works with assistive technologies that may not fully support JavaScript frameworks, works on older devices, and degrades gracefully when scripts fail. The GOV.UK Design System is built on this principle.

Server-side rendering for critical journeys: For transactional journeys (applying, submitting, paying), server-side rendering produces complete HTML pages that assistive technologies can parse reliably. Client-side rendered single-page applications can be made accessible but require significantly more effort to manage focus, announce state changes, and handle navigation. If you must use client-side rendering, ensure your framework has mature accessibility support (ARIA live regions, focus management, route announcements).

The GOV.UK Design System as your component library: Using the GOV.UK Design System means inheriting components that have been extensively tested with assistive technologies. This does not guarantee accessibility (you can still use the components incorrectly) but it gives you a solid foundation. Architecture decisions to use the Design System should be recorded as ADRs.

Multi-channel notification architecture: Design your notification system to support multiple channels from the start. GOV.UK Notify supports email, SMS, and letters. Allow users to set their preferred channel. For critical notifications (payment confirmations, decision outcomes), consider sending through multiple channels.

Structured content storage: Store content as structured data with semantic meaning rather than formatted HTML. This allows the same content to be rendered appropriately for different contexts — full web pages, simplified text for screen readers, plain text for SMS, large print for letters.

Accessible document generation: If your service generates documents (certificates, letters, decision notices), your document generation architecture must produce accessible outputs — tagged PDFs with correct reading order, properly structured headings, and alternative text for any images. Alternatively, provide HTML versions of all documents.

Performance as an accessibility concern: Slow services disproportionately affect users with cognitive disabilities, users on older devices, and users on limited data connections. Architecture decisions that improve performance (caching, CDN, efficient API design, optimised images) are accessibility decisions.

content.heading: Assisted Digital and Offline Access
content.body:
Not all users can use digital services independently. The GDS assisted digital guidance requires services to support users who need help — whether from a support agent over the phone, a face-to-face helper, or a family member assisting them.

Architecture for assisted digital requires: a mechanism for support agents to act on behalf of users (delegated access), the ability to start a journey in one session and complete it in another (save and return), and a support interface that allows agents to see what the user sees, understand where they are in the journey, and help them proceed.

The architecture must support assisted digital without compromising security. A support agent acting on behalf of a user should: be authenticated and authorised in their own right, have their actions audited separately from user actions, be able to help without knowing the user's password, and have access only to the information needed to provide assistance.

Offline access matters for services with users in areas of poor connectivity, or users who need to complete forms that require gathering information they do not have immediately available. Architecture patterns for offline include: progressive web apps with offline storage (allowing form completion without connectivity), save-and-return functionality (allowing users to save progress and return later when they have connectivity), and downloadable forms that can be completed offline and submitted later.

The Digital Inclusion Action Plan, published in February 2025, recognises that digital exclusion is a significant barrier to accessing public services. Architecture that assumes universal high-speed connectivity excludes millions of citizens. Design for the worst-case connectivity your users will experience — not just the connectivity available in your development office.

Paper fallback is still required for some services — a non-digital alternative for users who cannot use the digital service at all. Your architecture must accommodate paper submissions being entered into the digital system, either by support staff or through scanning and data extraction.

content.heading: Testing Accessibility at the Architecture Level
content.body:
Accessibility testing typically focuses on the interface — checking colour contrast, screen reader compatibility, and keyboard navigation. But architecture-level accessibility should also be verified.

Performance testing under constrained conditions: test your service on low-specification devices, slow network connections, and older browsers. If the architecture relies on heavy client-side processing, large JavaScript bundles, or high-bandwidth media, it may perform poorly for users on constrained devices — which correlates strongly with disability and digital exclusion.

Channel testing: verify that every user journey works through every supported channel. If you support phone assistance, test the full journey with a support agent. If you generate letters, verify they are readable. If you send notifications by SMS, verify the content makes sense within character limits.

Assistive technology testing: while primarily a development concern, architecture decisions affect what assistive technologies can do. If your architecture uses WebSockets for real-time updates, test whether screen readers announce those updates. If your architecture uses client-side state management, test whether screen readers maintain context when the page updates.

Document accessibility: if your architecture generates documents (PDFs, Word documents), verify they are accessible using automated and manual testing. Automated tools like PAC (PDF Accessibility Checker) can identify structural issues. Manual testing with a screen reader verifies reading order and content comprehension.

The GDS accessibility team recommends that services conduct a comprehensive accessibility audit at least once during beta, covering automated testing (which catches about 30% of issues), manual expert review (which catches structural and cognitive issues), and testing with real users who use assistive technologies. Architecture decisions should support all three — providing environments and tools for testing, and ensuring the architecture does not introduce barriers that are difficult to test for.

Full WCAG 2.2 validation requires manual testing with assistive technologies and expert accessibility review. Automated tools are a starting point, not a complete assessment.

content.heading: Common Accessibility Anti-Patterns in Architecture
content.body:
Certain architecture decisions create accessibility barriers that are expensive to fix later.

CAPTCHA as the only bot-protection mechanism: CAPTCHAs are notoriously inaccessible. Image-based CAPTCHAs exclude blind users. Audio CAPTCHAs are difficult for deaf users. Puzzle CAPTCHAs exclude users with motor impairments. Architecture alternatives include: rate limiting, invisible bot detection (behavioural analysis), and honeypot fields. If you must use a CAPTCHA, ensure your architecture supports an accessible alternative path.

Timeout without warning or extension: Sessions that expire silently after a fixed period exclude users who need more time — people using screen readers, people with cognitive disabilities, people using switch access. Architecture decisions about session management must include: warnings before timeout, the ability to extend sessions, and preservation of entered data if timeout occurs.

PDF-only document delivery: Generating only PDF documents excludes users whose assistive technology cannot parse the PDF correctly (which is common even with tagged PDFs). Architecture should support HTML document delivery as an alternative, or at minimum generate PDFs that meet PDF/UA (Universal Accessibility) standards.

Single-factor authentication without alternatives: If your authentication architecture requires a specific action (reading a code from a phone screen, clicking a link in an email), ensure alternatives exist for users who cannot perform that action. GOV.UK One Login provides multiple verification methods — use it rather than building your own single-method authentication.

Media without alternatives: An architecture that serves video content without captions, audio content without transcripts, or interactive visualisations without data tables excludes users with sensory impairments. Your content management architecture must support alternative formats as a first-class requirement.

Drag-and-drop as the only interaction pattern: WCAG 2.2's new criterion 2.5.7 (Dragging Movements) requires that any functionality using dragging has a single-pointer alternative. If your architecture includes file upload, form ordering, or visual workflow builders, ensure the underlying capability supports non-drag interaction methods.

The pattern across all these anti-patterns: providing only one way to do something. Accessible architecture provides multiple paths to the same outcome, allowing users to choose the path that works with their abilities.

workedExample.title: Redesigning a Grant Application Service for Accessibility
workedExample.context: A DESNZ grant application service was built 18 months ago using a React single-page application with client-side form validation. An accessibility audit has identified 47 WCAG 2.2 AA failures, including: dynamic content not announced to screen readers, form errors not associated with their fields, timeout without warning, and document uploads that only work via drag-and-drop. The development team estimates 12 weeks of remediation work. The Solution Architect is asked to assess whether the issues are fixable within the current architecture or require architectural change.
workedExample.approach:
The architect categorises the 47 failures into architecture-caused and implementation-caused issues.

Implementation-caused (32 issues): Missing ARIA attributes, insufficient colour contrast, missing form labels, images without alt text. These can be fixed within the current architecture by the development team. Estimated effort: 6 weeks.

Architecture-caused (15 issues): Dynamic content announcements require ARIA live regions that the current React component structure does not support cleanly. Form validation runs client-side only, meaning screen readers do not receive error summaries. The session timeout is enforced by the API with no warning to the client. Document upload uses a drag-and-drop library with no accessible alternative. File generation produces inaccessible PDFs.

The architect proposes targeted architecture changes:

1. Add a notification announcement component at the application root that manages ARIA live regions for all dynamic content across the application. This is a structural change to the React component hierarchy.

2. Move critical form validation to the server side, returning error summaries in the response that can be rendered as an accessible error summary component (following the GOV.UK Design System error pattern).

3. Redesign session management: the API sends a warning 5 minutes before timeout, the client displays an accessible modal with options to extend or save progress, and entered data is preserved to local storage in case timeout occurs.

4. Replace the drag-and-drop upload library with the GOV.UK Design System file upload component, which supports both click-to-select and drag-and-drop with appropriate keyboard and screen reader support.

5. Replace the PDF generation library with one that produces tagged PDF/UA documents, and add an HTML alternative for all generated documents.
workedExample.outcome: The combined remediation (implementation fixes + architecture changes) takes 10 weeks — less than the original 12-week estimate for implementation-only fixes, because the architecture changes resolve multiple issues simultaneously. Post-remediation audit finds 2 remaining minor issues (both advisory level). The service publishes an updated accessibility statement confirming WCAG 2.2 AA compliance. The architect records an ADR: 'Future DESNZ services will use the GOV.UK Design System with progressive enhancement and server-side validation as the default architecture, reducing accessibility remediation risk.'
workedExample.lessonsLearned: The original architecture choice (React SPA with client-side rendering and validation) was not inherently inaccessible, but it made accessibility significantly harder to achieve. Every accessibility feature had to be explicitly implemented rather than being available by default. The lesson for future services is clear: choosing the GOV.UK Design System with progressive enhancement provides accessibility by default, while choosing a client-side framework requires explicit accessibility engineering at every step. The architecture decision has a direct impact on the ongoing cost of maintaining accessibility compliance.

civilServiceScenario.title: The Service That Excluded 20% of Its Users
civilServiceScenario.background: A government service for applying for disability benefits was built with a complex multi-step form featuring conditional branching, file upload for medical evidence, and real-time eligibility checking. Post-launch analytics reveal that 20% of users who start the journey abandon it before submission. User research identifies that the primary causes of abandonment are: the form times out before users can complete it (users with cognitive disabilities need more time), the medical evidence upload only accepts drag-and-drop on desktop (excluding mobile users and users with motor impairments), the real-time eligibility check uses a visual progress indicator that screen readers cannot interpret, and the save-and-return feature requires email verification that some users cannot complete independently.
civilServiceScenario.challenge: The service is live and processing 5,000 applications per week. The 20% abandonment represents approximately 1,000 citizens per week who cannot access a benefit they may be entitled to. You must propose architecture changes that address the accessibility barriers without disrupting the live service.
constraints: The service is live and cannot have extended downtime
5,000 applications per week are being processed successfully and must not be disrupted
The development team has 4 developers and cannot grow in the short term
The medical evidence upload is a critical part of the journey — caseworkers need evidence to make decisions
The real-time eligibility check reduces caseworker workload by filtering ineligible applications early
The service assessment panel has formally noted the accessibility issues and required remediation within 6 months
The Equality and Human Rights Commission has received complaints about the service
Some users are being assisted by Citizens Advice staff who report the service is unusable with screen readers
The service is built on a bespoke framework — not the GOV.UK Design System
civilServiceScenario.yourRole: You are the Solution Architect tasked with proposing remediation that addresses the accessibility barriers within budget and timeline.
civilServiceScenario.discussion:
This scenario is particularly challenging because the service is actively excluding users from disability benefits — the very people who are most likely to have accessibility needs. The political and legal exposure is significant.

The architect must prioritise based on user impact: the session timeout and upload mechanism are likely causing the most abandonment because they completely block progress. The eligibility checker and save-and-return issues reduce usability but may not cause complete abandonment.

Architecture changes within £150,000 might include: extending the session timeout to 60 minutes with a 5-minute warning (relatively simple API change), adding a standard file picker as an alternative to drag-and-drop upload (replacing the upload component), making the eligibility check asynchronous (submit the form first, check eligibility after submission, notify the user of the result), and adding a phone number alternative for save-and-return verification (GOV.UK Notify can send verification codes by SMS).

The broader lesson is that building on a bespoke framework rather than the GOV.UK Design System was an architecture decision that created these problems. The Design System's components have been tested with assistive technologies — a bespoke framework has not. An ADR for future services should mandate the Design System unless there is a compelling justification.

practiceArtefact.description: Assess the following proposed architecture for accessibility risk: A new government service will use a React-based single-page application, WebSocket-based real-time notifications, biometric authentication (fingerprint/face), drag-and-drop workflow builder for internal caseworkers, and PDF-only document generation. For each architectural choice, identify the accessibility risk, the affected user group, and propose an accessible alternative or mitigation.
practiceArtefact.guidance: For each component, think about: which users would be excluded? Is there a legal obligation (WCAG 2.2 AA criterion) that this would breach? Is the accessibility risk fixable within this architecture, or does it require a different architectural approach? Propose alternatives that maintain the desired functionality while being accessible.
practiceArtefact.modelAnswer:
**Accessibility Architecture Risk Assessment**

| Architectural Choice | Accessibility Risk | Affected Users | WCAG Impact | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| React SPA | Dynamic content not announced to screen readers without explicit ARIA management | Blind and low-vision users | 4.1.3 Status Messages | Implement ARIA live regions with a centralised announcement component. Consider server-side rendering for critical transactional journeys. |
| WebSocket real-time notifications | Notifications may not be perceived by screen reader users or users with cognitive disabilities | Blind users, users with attention difficulties | 4.1.3 Status Messages | Implement an accessible notification queue with ARIA live regions (polite priority). Provide a notification history page for users who miss real-time alerts. |
| Biometric authentication only | Excludes users without biometric hardware, users with certain physical disabilities that prevent fingerprint/face scanning | Users with limb differences, older device users, users with facial conditions | Not directly a WCAG criterion but an Equality Act reasonable adjustment concern | Provide alternative authentication methods (password + 2FA, security key). Biometrics as an option, never the only method. |
| Drag-and-drop workflow builder | Excludes keyboard-only users, screen reader users, users with motor impairments | Users with motor impairments, blind users, users of switch access | 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (WCAG 2.2) | Provide a list-based alternative interface where workflows are constructed through sequential selection rather than spatial arrangement. |
| PDF-only documents | May be inaccessible to screen readers if PDFs are not tagged correctly; not responsive on mobile | Blind users, low-vision users, mobile users | 1.3.1 Info and Relationships, 1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence | Generate HTML versions as the primary format. If PDF required, ensure PDF/UA compliance with proper tagging, reading order, and alt text. |

**Overall Assessment:** HIGH RISK. Three of five architectural choices create barriers that breach specific WCAG 2.2 AA criteria. The biometric-only authentication raises Equality Act concerns. Recommend: adopt the GOV.UK Design System for the citizen-facing interface, provide authentication alternatives, offer both HTML and accessible PDF documents, and replace the drag-and-drop workflow builder with a list-based alternative for caseworkers.

reflectiveQuestions: Think about the last service you designed or reviewed. Were accessibility requirements treated as architecture constraints from day one, or as testing criteria applied at the end?
How would your architecture change if you designed for the hardest-to-serve user first — someone using a screen reader on a slow mobile connection with cognitive fatigue?
Has an accessibility audit of a service you architected ever revealed issues that were caused by architecture decisions rather than implementation mistakes? What were they?
How does your department ensure that third-party components and services meet accessibility requirements? Is this checked at the architecture selection stage or only after integration?
What would you change about your current architecture approach to make accessibility the default rather than an additional effort?

knowledgeCheck.question: What accessibility standard must UK public sector websites and applications meet?
options: WCAG 2.0 Level A
WCAG 2.1 Level AA
WCAG 2.2 Level AA
Section 508 compliance
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The Public Sector Bodies Accessibility Regulations 2018 require compliance with WCAG 2.2 at Level AA. This was updated from WCAG 2.1 following the publication of WCAG 2.2 in October 2023. The government guidance explicitly states that services must meet WCAG 2.2 AA standard.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why is accessibility an architecture concern rather than just a development concern?
options: Because architects are responsible for all aspects of the service
Because architecture decisions about technology selection, rendering approach, and content structure determine whether accessibility is achievable
Because accessibility testing can only be done by architects
Because WCAG standards are only relevant to system architecture, not to interface design
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Architecture decisions (technology selection, server-side vs client-side rendering, notification channels, authentication methods, document generation) determine whether the service can be made accessible at all. If the architecture makes accessibility difficult or impossible, no amount of front-end development effort will compensate.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which architecture approach provides the strongest default accessibility for government services?
options: A React single-page application with comprehensive ARIA implementation
Progressive enhancement using the GOV.UK Design System with server-side rendering
A native mobile application with platform accessibility APIs
A headless CMS with multiple front-end frameworks
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Progressive enhancement with the GOV.UK Design System provides accessibility by default because the Design System's components have been extensively tested with assistive technologies, and progressive enhancement ensures the core experience works without JavaScript. Other approaches can be made accessible but require explicit additional effort.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does WCAG 2.2 criterion 2.5.7 (Dragging Movements) require?
options: All drag-and-drop functionality must be removed from government services
Drag-and-drop must be tested with screen readers
Any functionality that uses dragging must have a single-pointer alternative that does not require dragging
Drag-and-drop must only be used for file uploads
knowledgeCheck.explanation: WCAG 2.2 criterion 2.5.7 requires that any functionality operated through dragging must also be operable through a single-pointer alternative (like clicking or tapping). Drag-and-drop is not prohibited — but it cannot be the only way to achieve the functionality. An accessible alternative must exist.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the architectural implication of the government's assisted digital requirement?
options: All services must be available by telephone only
The architecture must support delegated access where support agents can act on behalf of users
Services must be built in two separate versions — digital and non-digital
Assisted digital only applies to services for elderly users
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Assisted digital means support agents help users complete the digital journey. The architecture must support this through: delegated access (agents acting on behalf of users), a support interface showing the user's journey state, save-and-return (so users can start with an agent and finish independently), and audit trails separating agent actions from user actions.
